title: Packet Capture — tcpdump & Wireshark
summary: Capturing and reading raw traffic to debug what's actually happening on the wire, beyond what application logs show.

slides.markdown:
**Packet capture** — recording the raw bytes actually crossing a network interface — is the ground-truth tool when application logs disagree with what you're observing. `tcpdump` captures from the command line; `Wireshark` gives the same data a rich, browsable GUI.

- Logs tell you what the app *thinks* happened; a capture shows what actually went on the wire.
- Both tools use the same underlying capture library (libpcap) — the `.pcap` files are interchangeable.
- Reading a capture means recognizing TCP handshakes, retransmissions, and resets in the raw output.

slides.subTitle: Ground truth vs logs
slides.markdown:
Application logs are a filtered, after-the-fact story — they log what the app's code chose to log, at the layer the app operates. A packet capture instead shows **exactly what left or arrived on the wire**, including things no app log would mention: whether a TCP handshake completed, whether a packet was retransmitted, whether the *server* actually received a request the client logged as "sent successfully."

This matters most when logs at two ends of a connection disagree — a capture settles the disagreement with ground truth instead of guessing which log to trust.

slides.subTitle: Interfaces and filters
slides.markdown:
`tcpdump` captures on a network interface, with filters narrowing what it shows:

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 443
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.0.5
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 icmp
```

`-i` picks the interface (`any` captures all); filters combine with `and`/`or`. Without a filter, tcpdump dumps every packet — usually too much to read.

slides.subTitle: In tcpdump output
slides.markdown:
A TCP three-way handshake in `tcpdump` output looks like this:

```
12:00:01.001 IP client.51000 > server.443: Flags [S], seq 100
12:00:01.021 IP server.443 > client.51000: Flags [S.], seq 500, ack 101
12:00:01.022 IP client.51000 > server.443: Flags [.], ack 501
```

`[S]` is a SYN, `[S.]` is SYN-ACK, `[.]` is a plain ACK — that pattern *is* the handshake completing. Only a `[S]` with no `[S.]` reply means the connection never established. See [tcp-connection-management](tcp-connection-management).

slides.subTitle: Following a stream
slides.markdown:
**Wireshark** captures the same packets `tcpdump` would, but gives you a GUI to reconstruct and browse them meaningfully — most usefully, **Follow TCP Stream**, which reassembles every packet belonging to one connection into the actual data sent, in order, readable as a conversation rather than a scroll of individual packets.

That's the practical reason people reach for Wireshark over raw `tcpdump` output: seeing request/response bodies reassembled, color-coded by direction, is far faster than manually tracing sequence numbers across dozens of packet lines.

slides.subTitle: Isolating one conversation
slides.markdown:
Isolating one conversation out of a busy capture is the single most useful capture skill:

```bash
# Everything between exactly these two hosts
tcpdump -i any host 10.0.0.5 and host 10.0.0.9

# One TCP conversation by port pair
tcpdump -i any 'tcp port 443 and host 10.0.0.5'
```

In Wireshark, the equivalent is a display filter like `ip.addr==10.0.0.5 && tcp.port==443` — same idea, applied after capture instead of during it.

![Capturing at the client, at the server, or at a midpoint router each reveals a different slice of the same conversation](assets/capture-point-visibility.svg)

Where you capture changes what you can see: at the **client**, you see what left the NIC (not whether it arrived). At the **server**, you see what arrived (not the client's own retransmissions before that). At a **midpoint**, you see the path between, but may miss traffic that took a different route (asymmetric routing).

slides.subTitle: Retransmissions, resets, dup ACKs
slides.markdown:
Three signatures point at specific failure classes — see [tcp-reliability-flow-control](tcp-reliability-flow-control):

- **Retransmissions** — a segment sent more than once; the sender never got an ACK in time. Frequent ones on an idle link mean real packet loss.
- **RST packets** — an abrupt termination, often a firewall blocking traffic, or an app rejecting a connection.
- **Duplicate ACKs** — the receiver re-acking the same offset, signaling data arrived out of order — usually the first sign of a lost packet.

Recognizing these turns "something's wrong" into a concrete finding.

| | tcpdump | Wireshark |
|---|---|---|
| Interface | Command line | GUI |
| Shines at | Remote servers (SSH-only), scripting, quick filters | Deep visual inspection, stream reassembly |
| Typical workflow | Capture on a server, save to a `.pcap` file | Open that `.pcap` locally for analysis |

**How to decide:** capture with `tcpdump` wherever you have to (a headless server), analyze with Wireshark wherever you can — a common pattern is capturing then `scp`-ing the file to a laptop.

slides.subTitle: Wrong interface, "no traffic"
slides.markdown: A classic beginner mistake: running `tcpdump` on the wrong network interface (or filtering for the wrong host) and concluding **"there's no traffic — the connection never even left this machine."** A multi-homed server (multiple NICs, or a container with its own virtual interface) can have traffic flowing perfectly well on `eth1` while you're capturing on `eth0` and seeing nothing. Before concluding "no traffic," verify you're on the interface the traffic actually uses — `tcpdump -i any` captures every interface at once and sidesteps the guess entirely.
